or performance improvement is claimed.

The accumulator type's heap-bound marker is u32::MAX (4,294,967,295), not a
raised meter ceiling. The prelude fixture ran 6 chunks over 2 sweeps, wrote
6 rows, and produced [8, 12, 12] after a configuration change following the
first chunk. A prelude that exhausted heap parked with 0 committed chunks
and 0 rows written. The largest changed Rust source is 1,315 lines.

What the implementation taught: reassignment needs a loop-carried type join,
including paths that continue, while a fresh assignment has the new value's
own type. Recursively nesting an accumulator has no finite inferred type.
Heap-bound strings and lists can be written, with actual lengths checked by
the row validator, without claiming smaller bounds inside inline helpers.
A helper's early return must leave that helper's nested loops and preserve
the caller; a chunk's setup must run before even evaluating its scan prefix.
Quoted '-' also exposed a lexer-kind distinction the expression parser had
missed; it now remains a text literal.

## 2026-09-13 — Lane X: durable worker actions

Implemented LLP 3000.007 §9.2, ruling 11, phase C2. Quarry declares
`action name(args)` with typed arguments and an optional viewer rule; the
application supplies the TypeScript body. The generated API exposes
`Action<A, unknown>`. Admission records `_requests` transactionally once
per client id, keeps results private to the original principal and action,
and returns a settled result or a pending id after at most 25 seconds.
Replays survive store reopen and ignore replacement arguments. Action
results are bounded JSON outside Quarry's value model; no serialized value
form, meter ceiling or existing corpus case changed.

Service workers claim requests with a fresh non-renewable session for the
REQUEST's principal. The session ends at the shorter of its configured
lifetime and lease, defaults to 60 seconds, and is revoked on settlement.
A delegated session cannot become a worker credential, even when its
principal is a service seat. Settlement requires the claim's session token
in `x-snapback-action-lease`: this additional wire header fences a stale
attempt when the next worker uses the same service token. Expired leases
requeue; errors back off from 2 seconds to 5 minutes, at most 8 attempts;
`GiveUp` fails immediately. A lost settlement response leaves the lease
recoverable; invalid JSON results fail without repeatedly running the handler.

Both clients expose `act` without prediction, mutation receipts or device
outbox entries. A known offline client returns `denied: E_OFFLINE`; an
uncertain transport response preserves a pending id for an explicit retry.
React's `useAction` keeps `last` on the newest invocation and respects its
client/component lifetime. **`Act<R>` is a new card word needing the author's
ruling under LLP 2000.000 §8**, as the lane brief requires. Its done/failed/
pending union also has `{ denied, id }` for refusal before admission. The
implementation and the actions card expose that choice for review; no
ruling on the new word is implied by this entry.

`dev` supervises `snapback/worker.ts` or `.mjs` with Node 24 and one printed
`service:worker` token, restarts crashes with backoff and stops its own child
on exit. `doctor` reports the worker file and queue counts. Chat's action
`invite(email: text <=200)` mints a session for `member:<email>` and returns
only the principal. Its old membership mutation is now `addMember`, with
all callers updated. The Expo starter copies the worker together with the
schema. Data-only chat fixtures and witnesses exclude the worker file;
copying it into temporary projects without its dependencies had introduced
an unwanted worker and a server-shutdown race in those tests.

15,787.616125 ms. Its action round trips, including a viewer write and read,
were 10.44 ms online and 11.07 ms through the process device; a one-second
pending wait took 1,004.26 ms. In the final Linux suite those measurements
were 20.33 ms, 14.22 ms and 1,003.64 ms. These are individual observations,
not percentiles or improvement claims. The core proves 60,000 ms default
and 120,000 ms configured viewer lifetimes, terminal expiry on attempt 8,
and exactly 2 attempts after a lost settlement. Offline action POSTs and
queued device entries are both 0. The dev probe observes 1 crash/restart,
1 printed service token, and doctor counts 0 queued / 0 running / 2 done /
1 failed. Local wasm: 1,441,096 B raw / 405,953 B gzip; Linux wasm:

and preserve lazy reads; seek keys/bounds must preserve source evaluation

metadata belongs to a projected row, including through named spreads, not
to its enclosing ordinary object. Defaults need both the engine boundary
and the insert expression's returned image to agree.

## 2026-09-14 — lane U: sync bodies and bounded link-loss detection

Moved the shared client's sync request to `POST /sync` with JSON
`{ from, limit, after, stream, pending }`, removed the GET route, and
updated the scale witness and HTTP/cursor fixtures. The native opener
already delegates HTTP to the shared client; the labelled mock has no
wire request to migrate. The body ceiling is **262,144 B** with one
oversize outcome, **HTTP 413 / E_INPUT**, including chunked requests and
CORS. That allows **256 × 128-byte IDs** even at **6 encoded bytes per
byte**, plus a cursor; malformed fields use **400 / E_INPUT**. No request-line
or meter ceiling was raised, no serialized value form or engine changed.

At watermark **1091**, the old request lines for **232 / 233 / 256**
ordinary 26-byte IDs were **8,171 / 8,206 / 9,011 B**; at 128 bytes they
were **31,835 / 31,972 / 35,123 B**. Every POST line is **19 B**; its
bodies are **6,794 / 6,823 / 7,490 B** for ordinary IDs and
**30,458 / 30,589 / 33,602 B** for maximum-length IDs. The real host
regression checks both lengths, the old parser boundary, **262,144 B**
admitted and **262,145 B** refused, declared/chunked bodies and malformed
fields. On each device store it correlates and terminally acknowledges
**232, 233, and 273** writes (the last has a **256-ID** window and a
**17-ID** tail), with **37** snapshot rows over **6** pages and **5**
cursors, no dropped/duplicate IDs, one terminal notification per write,
and an empty outbox. Across the two stores: **1,476** receipts and
**1,476** terminal writes.

Held change responses now send JSON-whitespace heartbeats every **2 s**;
both client tiers race response progress against **4 s** of silence.
Native fetch without response streaming uses polls of at most **2 s**
with the same watchdog. Browser offline/online hints are registered and
removed with the client; authenticated `/probe` remains the recovery
condition. README, `Link`, and the guide document detection within **5 s**
while polling on a running host, with notifications deferred during host
suspension. The real TCP proxy drops bytes without closing the held poll;
final-suite detection times after cuts at **500 / 5,000 / 15,000 ms**:
wasm **3,503.941 / 3,007.609 / 3,023.060 ms**, native
**3,502.317 / 3,006.491 / 3,028.957 ms**. The test retains request start,
cut, rejection and notification times and checks recovery. Healthy idle
polls, a buffered native response, a fetch that ignores abort, browser
hints, cleanup, and revocation after the first heartbeat are covered.

Learned: tiny_http's absolute **5 s** write phase cannot include an idle
**25 s** response. The minimal vendor addition (**22 lines**) writes and
flushes complete frames with the existing deadline, retaining the request
until its terminator so a later request cannot start the next header
phase too early. It aborts incomplete streams. Two Rust HTTP tests prove
healthy pipelining across idle frames and refusal of a stalled frame;
auth is rechecked before final JSON, including after heartbeats started.
The early regression run caught that phase mismatch; fixture repairs used
unique native outbox sequences, avoided closing a wasm core twice, and
explicitly enabled identity for the revocation test.

## 2026-09-14 — Lane A: dev loopback Argon2 capacity follows the host

Applied LLP 3000.007 §14 ruling 9: admission snapshots the host's available
parallelism once, clamps it to 2–16, and uses that capacity only for `dev`
loopback password work. The shared bounded semaphore still refuses excess
work with retryable `E_RATE_LIMIT`; `serve` and non-loopback requests keep
two slots. This host reports 18 available cores and dev prints
`Argon2 slots: 16 on this host` on stderr. Minute counters, Argon2
parameters, the engine meter, serialized values and client code are unchanged.
The README and personas card explain both capacities; ruling 9 gains one
dated application sentence without changing its existing text.

The new HTTP regression parks eight simultaneous sign-ins before their
Argon2 work, proves a query completes while they are parked, then verifies
all eight sessions succeed without a refusal. On hosts with fewer than
eight available cores it tests the smaller physical capacity. The existing
third-request refusal test now runs as `serve` with a real guest session
instead of a dev persona, covering both signup and login and the retryable
flag. The semaphore regression fills each admission class, refuses the
next permit, and proves released permits can be reused.

Measured eight existing accounts over loopback HTTP on unoptimized Cargo
dev binaries, before at `0d7b77bb3c577366ac81bf159e57524c613c9e12` and after
this change. Account creation is outside the clock; eight request threads
start together. Three trials per mode, measured sequentially after the
baseline suite finished (milliseconds):

| Mode | Before trials | After trials | Before → after median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One attempt per login | 256.980, 248.675, 253.208 | 261.905, 290.482, 314.969 | 253.208 → 290.482 |
| All eight complete, retry refusals every 25 ms | 1137.052, 1033.687, 1032.919 | 339.553, 355.558, 358.707 | 1033.687 → 355.558 |

The first row is **2 successes / 6 rate refusals before, 8 / 0 after** in
every trial, so its elapsed times are not equal amounts of completed work.
The second row completes eight in every trial: 115, 108, 106 refusals
before and zero after, a 2.907× median completion speedup with this retry
policy. An earlier baseline measured alongside the busy base suite took
1677.680 ms median to complete eight, illustrating shared-host variance.
These are local debug-build observations, not packaged throughput claims.
The measurement program and raw results are in `/tmp/snapback-lane-A-auth/`.

Targeted tests: auth **3 passed**, HTTP **18 passed**, compiled guide
**8 passed**, client seams **4 passed**, all with zero failures. The full
suite's first changed-tree run caught the client-seams assertion expecting
the old startup sentence; its one-line expectation now checks a printed
2–16 slot count. That test file is the only addition to the brief's named
file scope. The final full suite took **30 s**: **303 Rust passed,
0 failed, 1 ignored; 9 fixture tests passed; 111 client tests passed,
1 failed**. All builds and typechecks passed. The sole remaining failure
is Chromium SIGABRT before the React assertions, reproduced alone on this
tree and on the untouched base above. The base suite also encountered an
HTTP startup timeout and a worker timeout (the latter repeated alone);
both passed in the final full suite. A green outside-sandbox Chromium run
remains the lead's, not a green-suite claim from this lane.

Learned: lifting minute counters did not remove the two-slot correction
loop; concurrent admission needed its own regression, independent of the
implementation's selected capacity. Startup text is also an exercised
surface, with an assertion outside the server crate. Modified source files
remain below 1,500 lines (maximum 1,464); this journal was already 3,054
lines, and its prior entries are preserved verbatim. No commit, push, tag
or publication.

## 2026-09-14 — Lane D: the silent dev exit was a lost SQLite shared-memory lock

Closed [the schema/backfill exit ticket](../issues/closed/20260913-snapback4-dev-exits-without-diagnostic-during-schema-change.md).
The original macOS crash report identifies PID 62517, parent 62515, as
SIGBUS in a writable 32 KiB mapped file, with `FS pagein error: 22 Invalid
argument`. The two recorded PIDs were a launcher and its binary, not evidence
of two independent binary crashes. The permission helper opened and closed
SQLite's SHM file after SQLite had locked it; POSIX discarded the process's
locks, allowing the CLI backfill's SQLite opener to truncate a mapping the
server still used. Existing files now get chmod by path; new databases still
start at 0600. The only store change is its permission-setup call. No engine
write path, value form, ceiling, client implementation or language form changed.

Seven fresh SQLite reproduction attempts used the retained Clique scale
log's 49,200 post/set-repost feed entries, changing the public counter to a
repost-only source at 24,600 entries, with replay, reads and CLI backfill
concurrent. Two unchanged-base and two published 0.2.6 attempts crashed with
SIGBUS; three fixed attempts completed, with zero request failures and 1,000
backfilled rows each, in 9.237, 10.765 and 9.143 s. The first 0.2.6 attempt
looked for the adoption line on stderr when that pin printed it on stdout;
the retained line and the corrected repeat confirm generation 2. These are
focused host reproductions, not a replay of all 167,157 app/auth/media actions.
Commands and raw logs remain under `/private/tmp/lane-d/`.

Eleven Rust regressions cover cross-process database/SHM lock retention with
0600 permissions, memory and SQLite adoption waiting behind replay, the real
watcher and CLI backfill, a backfill parking after 200 committed chunks then
completing after correction, invalid source keeping the old generation,
startup refusals, off-thread unwind and abort panics, a real truncated-mapping
SIGBUS while holding a mutex, signals for both verbs, and app-worker cleanup.
The watcher also takes its initial stamp before compilation so an edit just
after the listening URL is not missed. `dev`/`serve` now print generation,
reason and a stable code on stderr for exits, panics, signals and background
thread stops; fatal signal reporting does not lock the engine or allocate.
The README and refusals card explain these codes and the limits for SIGKILL,
power loss or unwritable stderr. Without a worker, signals retain immediate
OS termination; with a worker, INT/TERM/HUP allow the existing child cleanup.

Targeted checks: lifecycle 11 passed; compiled guide 8 passed; local-client
and periphery 16 passed. Final blocking suite: 45 s; 312 Rust passed, 0 failed,
1 ignored; 9 fixture tests passed; 111 client tests passed, 1 failed. Chromium
SIGABRT before React assertions reproduces alone and on 60 tracked files
verified byte-identical to base `0d7b77bb3c577366ac81bf159e57524c613c9e12`,
Node 24.18.0. Earlier full runs took 122 and 38 s and exposed an introduced
100 ms shutdown delay in workerless servers; a reused-port test reached the
exiting server. Restoring immediate termination fixed that regression; no
client test was edited. The lead's outside-sandbox Chromium rerun remains.
`ref-check` is green. Modified source stays under 1,500 lines; this journal
was already 3,054 lines and remains append-only. No commit, push, tag or publish.

Learned: a Rust mutex cannot replace the OS locks SQLite uses across processes.
Permission tightening must preserve descriptor ownership, and a native signal
needs its own diagnostic path; a panic hook alone would not have explained this
crash. The original report could be attributed from the OS receipt before any
engine change was necessary.

## 2026-09-14 — CU2: retained history survives replacement acquisition (LLP 3000.007 §18.2)

Reproduced against base **518891fd1cc67b969a6f57b683e80efadc89b612** with
self-synced members, conversations and messages all retaining delivered
history, **26 messages**, a **25-row** message horizon and a local
`last 50 by byTime` read. The new regression is
`crates/snapback4-device/tests/retained_history.rs`; its ten tests were
**0 passed / 10 failed** against the base implementation. The paired
physical-store count matters: the actual deletion is
`crates/snapback4-device/src/device.rs:427` **at that base**, where replacement
application calls `tx.clear_rows()` and reinstalls only staged acquisition.
The server's horizon re-evaluation did not send message deletions. A live
scope itself already preserved the rows.

Both SQLite and memory produced these message counts; reopening each
store preserved the same result. The fixed replacement is also tested with
**15 unrelated public rows**, forcing a multi-page snapshot after leaving;
partial pages remain private.

| Path | Before leave | Base after | Fixed after | Local completeness before → after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Live scope | 25 | 25 | 25 | false → false |
| New paged snapshot from zero after leave | 25 | 0 | 25 | false → false |
| Snapshot catch-up starting after leave | 25 | 0 | 25 | false → false |
| Snapshot staged before leave, then log catch-up across leave | 25 | 25 | 25 | false → false |
| Logical membership expiry, appended scope without a sweep | 25 | 25 | 25 | false → false |

The unbounded control holds **26 rows**, with `complete: true` before and
after: the base also lost those **26 → 0** on replacement and catch-up
starting after leave, while the fix keeps **26 → 26** on every path. Thus
replacement loss is not specific to horizons. Rejoin acquires **25 current
images**, keeps the already delivered older image outside that acquisition,
and leaves **26 distinct rows** even after duplicate page application and
another paged snapshot; the never-delivered oldest row stays absent. An
explicit catch-up deletion leaves **24 rows**, and a later snapshot keeps
**24**. Predicted insertion, edit and deletion are not promoted to history:
replacement preserves the **25 confirmed images**. Media home authority is
retired on the staged scope and stays retired on resnapshot; reacquisition
activates it again, on both stores.

Built the fix by seeding snapshot staging with delivered-history rows and
overlaying their confirmed bases beneath predictions before acquisition.
Incoming puts replace those images; explicit deletes still remove them;
scopes preserve text and retire media authority. Staging distinguishes a
newly acquired image from a retained one, so publication does not authorize
revoked media. Tables without media keep their constant-work retained scope
path. No server partition filtering, acquisition limit, completeness rule,
meter ceiling, value-model serialization, or existing corpus case changed.
The sync card and README §3 now state the acquisition/retention distinction.
The exhausted horizon stays `complete: false`; the whole-group control
without a horizon stays `complete: true`. The existing rule cannot certify
an exhausted horizon merely because a small group happened to fit, and no
new coverage receipt or count-based completeness claim was introduced.

The browser evidence taught a second lesson: **0 rows / complete: true** is
not proof that the device store was cleared. In these regressions the local

## 2026-09-14 — CU2b: left history is the online answer; held snapshots replace (LLP 3000.007 §18.2)

Continued CU2 at base **09bbd95e7b7caed30ae2e281e187a28ee443b222**. The real
client regression first reproduced the builder-visible failure on that
unchanged base: **0 passed / 2 failed**, wasm and process device. Its output:

```text
R5 wasm online left: rows=0, complete=true; held: rows=26, complete=true
R5 process online left: rows=0, complete=true; held: rows=26, complete=true
```

The seam is the existing snapshot audience calculation, factored without
changing its rule or row filtering. The first snapshot page adds `held`, a map
from each delivered-history synced table to the viewer's current audience
prefixes, including an empty list when none are held. A stream page adds
`joined`, only the prefixes of this viewer's current grants whose joins are
on that page; an empty rejoin must clear left state without a row image.
Both fields use plain wire values and carry no row image or another
principal's groups. `local.ts` already forwards the whole page as a record,
so there is no separate transport parser to update. The server's current
readable-image filter is unchanged.

The device persists held/left state in its existing transaction metadata,
including groups with no delivered rows. Snapshot candidates and membership
state stay private together until publication; catch-up can mark a group
left between pages before its current rows were acquired. Only acquired
images or confirmed candidates of left groups publish. A held group therefore
replaces its rows with the snapshot's current acquisition, and an absent
server deletion cannot be copied back as a held row. Predictions are still
replaced by their confirmed bases before retention; explicit deletions and
media-home revocation keep their existing behavior. Reopen preserves the
state; clear/generation reset clears it with the partition.

The shared interpreter asks the device about a scan's evaluated prefix.
When it pins a left delivered-history group, its result keeps the existing
completeness rule but carries `retained: true`, and that horizon is not an
`unknown` fact. This is an internal device outcome, alongside `unknown`;
`contract.ts` and `Read<R>` are unchanged. `local.ts` consumes it at the
fallback shared by one-shot reads and watches, online and offline. A read
that does not pin a group, including a scan across all conversations, keeps
today's fallback. Held incomplete reads also keep their server fallback.
No acquisition limit, log backfill, meter ceiling, value-model serialization,
search form, `check`, `--fix`, or `processDevice` implementation changed.

Both stores produced the same physical/read counts and states:

| Path (SQLite and memory each) | Rows before → after | Complete after | Unknown / retained after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 held deletion while away, replacement | 25 → 25 | false | true / false |
| R2 unseen removal, replacement | 25 → 25 | false | false / true |
| R3 live removal, later replacement | 25 → 25 | false | false / true |
| R4 live rejoin, duplicate page | 25 → 26 distinct | false | true / false |
| R4 subsequent held replacement | 26 → 25 | false | true / false |
| Removal between snapshot pages plus catch-up | 25 → 25 | false | false / true |
| Unbounded whole-group leave/replacement/reopen | 26 → 26 | true | false / true |
| Confirmed delete, then left replacement | 24 → 24 | false | false / true |
| Predicted insert/edit/delete, left replacement | 25 confirmed → 25 | false | false / true |

R1 deletes visible `m25`; it remains absent, while ordinary snapshot
acquisition supplies `m00`, leaving 25 current rows. R4 still acquires exactly
25 puts on rejoin without duplication, but CU2's assertion that a *held*
replacement kept a 26th old row was the over-retention defect: it now expects
25 and excludes `m01` outside that horizon. Every CU2 scenario remains in the
suite. A 10-row page of the left group remains complete; full exhausted
horizon reads stay incomplete. The existing conservative rule is unchanged:
no coverage receipt or count-based completeness claim was introduced.

R5 wasm watch: rows=25, complete=false; offline left: rows=25; revoked server: rows=0

## 2026-09-14 — CU4: literal defaults interpret old images; check assesses the dev store

Built LLP 3000.007 §18.3. A required literal default is additive and fills
absent fields through the existing row-materialization path, before reads,
rule probes, validation, constraints, index keys and the wire. Adoption keeps
the stored image unchanged; it rebuilds index entries from the interpreted
image. A device keeps old images through a safe literal-default addition,
including on reopen with a new backend, while a changed generation still
invalidates native code and requests a snapshot. Both stores build, replace
and delete index entries using the same interpreted values. Optional defaults
keep their insert-only meaning: an absent optional still reads null.

`check` now opens the dev database read-only (or the explicit `--store`),
compares its active generation with the compiled schema in one read snapshot,
and reports each failed successor step as `E_ADOPT` at the declaration's site.
Atomic activation uses the same assessment and step message/rewrite. Checked
narrowing whose existing values already fit still adopts. Required `now` and
`viewer` additions refuse populated tables and adopt empty ones; insert
context is unchanged. The existing runtime codes did not describe this
located schema-adoption refusal, so `E_ADOPT` has its own `why` explanation.
The README's column text, Schema evolution paragraph and types card say so.

Measured scenarios use **3 old rows**, **0 adoption row rewrites** (a SQLite
trigger refuses any attempted rewrite), **0 new partition events**, and
**3 matches** on the newly added default-column index. Five required literal
kinds (bool, int, text, enum and decimal minor units) and one optional default
are checked on each server row: **18 field assertions**. SQLite and memory
devices each exercise live adoption and reopen with the successor, **4 device
scenarios**, each reading the same **3 old images** without a new snapshot;
their persisted images still lack the new column. The empty-table insert
controls read `now` as **1234** and `viewer` as **dev:alice**. Unique-index and
cap refusals also see the materialized value, and rule residual equalities
read it from the old image.

Before, the successor said:

```text
column messages.tombstone is added as required; existing rows must already carry it
```

The runtime refusal was `E_INPUT: messages.tombstone is required (bool)`.
After, the additive step says:

```text
column messages.tombstone is added with default false; rows written before it read false
```

For required contextual defaults the new messages are:

```text
column messages.at is added as required with default now; existing rows would read the adoption's clock
column messages.author is added as required with default viewer; existing rows would read the adoption's viewer
```

The text `check` output, verbatim (exit **1**):

```text
schema.q:3:3 — E_ADOPT: column messages.at is added as required with default now; existing rows would read the adoption's clock
  rewrite: at: time ? or at: time default <literal>; otherwise backfill existing rows before making the column required
  guide: types

check: 1 problem
```

The viewer rewrite is `author: principal ? or author: principal default
<literal>; otherwise backfill existing rows before making the column required`.
The live dev regression verifies that its refusal contains the exact message
and rewrite produced by check, then successfully adopts the literal default.

The important discovery was that the two stores previously did different
things to absent fields: SQLite persisted optional nulls during adoption,
while memory filled every missing column with null and a generation change
dropped all rows. Making a literal default mean the same thing everywhere
required keeping the raw image separate from its interpretation, including
when rebuilding or deleting an index entry. New optional text constraints
remain additive; caps can bind the materialized default group and must be
checked. No parser, client-package implementation, meter ceiling, serialized
value form or existing conformance case changed.

A final old-image regression covers a predicted row carrying `pending: true`.
SQLite now preserves that metadata while validating only schema columns;
the memory store already retained the mark. Both stores keep the raw image
and give it one match in the new default index: **2 additional device-store
scenarios**, **6 device scenarios total**.

## 2026-09-14 — lane W5: charge a uniform verdict by rule shape

Built the fifth-check disposition of LLP 3000.007 §17. A page verdict
from the pinned prefix charges the rule's static probe allowance once on
both outcomes, including the probes that short-circuit evaluation skipped.
The counter moved unchanged from write-target reservation into `rules.rs`:
`exists` costs **1**, `created` with residual equalities **1**, a bare
`created` fact **0**, `and`/`or` sum their children, and `not` keeps its
child's allowance. The reviewed two-probe shapes therefore cost **2**.
W4's aborting-page attempt still costs **1 examined unit** before the
verdict, with no candidates fetched before an allowed verdict. Capped
queries gain no attempt charge; a denied verdict restores hidden expiry
before its allowance can cut the query. No ceiling or serialized form changed.

The named denied regression compares **8 pairs**: `and` and its negated
`or` mirror, empty/hidden and equality mismatch/match, **0** or **8191**
prelude probes. Permits are empty in every world; the equality pair keeps
the same secret and varies only `enabled`. Another **8 pairs** exercise
true verdicts with a fixed target row. The shared helper compares all
**7 meters**, first/retry serializer bytes, receipt, committed source and
maintain deltas, effects, stream, snapshot, and admission/reopen/settlement
on **2 device stores**. Every world retains its starting source state.

Measured meter vectors, identical within every pair (the `and`/`or` and
existence/equality variants have the same numbers):

| Verdict and prelude | examined | index_entries | rule_probes | steps | heap_bytes | output_bytes | rows_written |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Denied, 0, sent with constant 7 | 1 | 0 | 2 | 5 | 0 | 9 | 0 |
| Allowed, 0, sent with constant 7 | 2 | 0 | 2 | 5 | 384 | 9 | 0 |
| Either, 8191, E_BOUND on rule probes | 8192 | 0 | 8193 | 32767 | 2096896 | 0 | 0 |

The query control covers both verdicts at probe ceilings **1** and **8192**,
with **2 probes** charged and **0** candidate examinations at the cut;
with room it examines **0** denied candidates or **1** allowed candidate.
A hidden expiring probe contributes no `next_expiry` on a denied query,
even when the allowance exceeds the ceiling. The lesson is that a verdict
can be uniform while its executed branch count is not: metering must use
schema shape at this boundary, not pad a state-dependent charge afterward.

The existing membership suite asserted a zero-cost false query verdict;
its assertion and two-line comment now expect **1 probe** for either
verdict. This is the one additional test file touched beyond the brief's

## 2026-10-08 — Quarry differential testing, slice C: the server against the device

LLP 3000.035 §5.1 oracle 4 is in `snapback4-difftest` (`src/devices.rs`,
`src/device_writes.rs`, `run-devices`). Each case runs on a server engine and on
two devices, the native SQLite store at a file path and the memory store. Both
devices come up the way the client brings them up. The backend is the
`/schema` reply as JSON text. Then one `local.ts::syncRound`: `sync_state`, `/sync`
snapshot pages built as `serve_sync.rs` builds them, `observe_store`, `apply`
through `call_text`, catch-up stream. Nothing is written into a device store
directly.

The device's published answers are compared on the whole outcome record:
`complete` with `unknown` false, and known refusals. The only exceptions are
the device's `seq` (always 0) and the server-only delivery manifest. Other reads
are counted by reason, and in this generator every one is `online-only-*`.
Writes go through `admit`. A device refusal must equal the server's. A
predicted row must equal the committed one, less its `pending` marker. After
`settle` and a sync round, the device must answer as the server does.

The device has no ceiling input. Low ceilings reach it only through `call`'s
`spent` ledger, which this run used. No shipped crate changed.

100,000 cases in 875 s with 8 workers on a loaded M-series Mac (load 90–120):

- 58,499 reads compared per store with zero disagreements; at the default
  ceilings all seven meter fields agree.
- 757,317 low-ceiling positions per store: 16,920 SQLite-device disagreements
  and 29,632 memory-device disagreements, all heap or step accounting.
- 2,282 writes compared per store, with 56 disagreeing; 2,967 convergences, all
  passing.

The heap findings are the device half of the 2026-10-08 heap ruling. The device
interpreter reads a non-uniform-rule table through a per-candidate ~18 KB
decoder reservation, so both stores show it. The memory store prices scans
without SQLite's page scratch. In both, the final charge agrees and the peak
does not. Their nine signatures route to the open heap ticket.

The write finding is new: a device predicts an insert whose caller-supplied id
belongs to a row outside its partition, and the server refuses it `E_RULE`
(`issues/20261008-snapback4-device-predicts-insert-over-an-unheld-id.md`).

Three planted device faults were each caught, then reverted with the shipped
crates verified clean:

- memory scan ties reversed: 32 read disagreements;
- a complete page's last row dropped: 120 per store;
- predicted writes refused: 25 per store.

The memory store is exercised natively, with the core's `sqlite` feature on,
not as the wasm artifact. The nightly runner adds `run-devices` to its
calibration and campaign.

## 2026-10-08 — Quarry in Lean, Stage 2: a small core with its security proofs

LLP 3000.035 §5.2's model is in `snapback4/lean/`. It is a Lake project
pinned to Lean 4.34.1, with no Mathlib. `./check.sh` builds it in about 15 s
cold and under 1 s warm. The script refuses any `sorry`, `admit`,
`native_decide` or `axiom`, and audits 38 headline theorems for standard
axioms only. It also runs 30 hand-written examples taken from the guide
cards. All 30 agree.

The model was written from the language card, the guide cards, the `why`
pages and the LLPs. The interpreter, binder, `value.rs`, `key.rs` and the
device crate were not read. Each point the documents leave open is in
`lean/OPEN.md` with the model's choice: 30 points, 3 of them confirmed by a
document or corpus case. The engine has not been consulted on any of them.
The points most likely to disagree with it are these:

- R1: a probe inside a rule sees rows its own table's read rule hides.
- R2: an unnamed `update <- R` judges both old and next.
- V2: null sorts before every other kind.
- C2: a page that fills exactly has `next: null` when no candidate follows.
- W1–W4: precedence among refusal codes.
- W2: an insert of a row its writer cannot read returns null.

**What is proved**, over the executable big-step semantics:

- The scalar order is a total order. Keys are ordered lexicographically, and
  the order agrees with an order-preserving, self-delimiting key encoding.
- Scan order is determined by key order: permuting the stored rows changes
  no page.
- A query's whole outcome is a function of the viewer's visible rows. This
  covers data, `complete`, `next`, refusal and unavailability. Every
  returned row and every cursor passes its read rule. `count` is exactly the
  number of visible matches. `exists` is true exactly when a visible row
  matches. A hidden insert changes no query.
- Write authority holds for each write and for whole mutations, as a chain
  of authorized steps.
- A page that reports `complete` returned exactly the first N qualifying
  visible rows. A cut page's rows, followed by its continuation's, equal the
  uncut page. That is oracle 2, now a theorem.
- `true or e` skips `e` for every `e`, and `identity(1) + identity(2) = 3`.
- Hoare rules for each statement form are sound.

Four planted model faults each made `lake build` fail:

- a cut page reported complete;
- an eager `or`;
- a dropped insert-rule check;
- a leaking view.

**Next is the emitter and harness lane.** `lean/README.md` sketches the case

## 2026-10-08 — S3: long-wait capacity on the HTTP host (LLP 3000.036 §6 A)

Charlie asked for "another round of changes" and then for far more than 32
held waits. The RFC's "now" set landed: `dev` and `serve` take
`--long-waits` (default **1,024**, was 32; at most 4,096),
`--long-waits-per-principal` (default 16) and `--claim-waits` (default 32),
each also as `SNAPBACK4_*`. Service workers' claim polls left the viewers'
pool for their own class. A full pool answers 503 `E_STREAMS` with
`Retry-After: 2` through a new vendored `refuse_overload_with` (same single
nonblocking write); a principal past its share gets 429 `E_STREAMS` with
`Retry-After: 5`, refused at once after authentication, never queued. The
connection cap is now derived (128 + both pools, 1,184 by default); startup
states the sizes and the descriptor need, refuses explicit sizes the NOFILE
limit cannot carry and lowers a default that does not fit. The JS client's
change feed treats `E_STREAMS` as a pause: it stays online, waits
Retry-After, then polls without `wait` at that pace for 30 s.

Measuring before choosing the number found what the RFC's estimates missed.
With only the pools raised, 1,024 held polls cost 232 KiB each (six
descriptors: each kept a detached SQLite reader) and one commit took 1.36 s
to answer them all; at 4,096 only 268 had answered after 20 s. Two herds:
every woken poll reopened a reader under the engine lock, and the engine's
FIFO lock (`serve_lock.rs`) woke *every* queued thread on each release, so a
thousand polls re-entering at once did quadratic wakeups (2,048 re-polls took
6.3 s; `sample` put 13,000 of 13,400 mutex-wait samples in `FairMutex::admit`
from `changes::serve`). Fixed in the same landing: each queued ticket parks on
its own condvar and a release wakes only the next; a parked poll holds no
reader; held polls woken by the same publication at the same cursor share
one answer read on a pooled reader (at most a second old, never below the
cursor; entry and unheld polls always read the store, which keeps the
finding-5 regression honest). Custom 512 KiB worker stacks were tried and dropped: RSS is touched
pages, and the action path can recurse.

`scripts/measure-long-waits.py` on the M5 (release, `dev --fresh`, one
principal, `wait=25&heartbeat=1`, after the review fold): per held poll about
85 KiB RSS, two threads, four descriptors. 256 / 1,024 / 2,048 / 4,096 held:
36 / 98 / 196 / 339 MiB, 521 / 2,057 / 4,105 / 8,201 threads; `/q` p50
0.20 / 0.21 / 0.33 / 0.61 ms while held; one commit answers all in
6 / 21 / 58 / 334 ms (persona) and 58 / 237 / 497 / 1,525 ms (bearer, which
rechecks each session); all re-poll at once in 74 / 38 / 94 / 416 ms
(persona) and 21 / 82 / 224 / 811 ms (bearer). 1,024 is the default because it keeps commit fan-out near a
quarter second with bearer sessions and threads (about 2,300) under systemd's
default `TasksMax`; 4,096 is the measured ceiling, near Darwin's 16,384
threads per process. Opening thousands of fresh connections at once overflows
Darwin's 128-entry listen backlog (about 300 resets at 4,096), which clients
retry. Tens of thousands of idle streams remain the evented-parking step.

Tests: a full viewer pool refuses `E_STREAMS` while short requests and unheld
polls progress; one principal's share is refused at once and released with
its polls; workers' claims and viewers' waits cannot starve each other in
either direction; eight held polls woken by one commit take fewer than eight reads;
capacity flags, environment and bounds; the client feed degrades and is paced
by Retry-After against a real `dev --long-waits-per-principal 1`. Existing
admission, overload, lifecycle and route-capacity tests moved to the split
classes. `E_STREAMS` is in `guide::CODES` with the wire card's defining
paragraph; SERVER.md "Long-wait capacity", README, CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md
and LLP 3000 / 3000.036 record the knobs and the measurement.

Blind review (GPT-6 Astra, xhigh, read-only, concurrency brief): **NOT READY**,
three findings, all folded. (1) MATERIAL: a cached answer could be older than
a commit the client already knew (committed, not yet published, as `/seed`
does between commit and publish), so a new poll could report a lower head and
trip the client's store-restore check. Entry and unheld polls now always read
the store; only polls woken by a publication share an answer, which is read
after that publication and so after the poll's entry. Regression: a new poll
after an unpublished commit reports it. (2) MATERIAL: a pooled reader can
predate an adoption that has committed but not yet replaced the pool, and its
`E_GENERATION` would have stopped the client feed. A failed pooled read (and a
failed pooled bearer recheck) is now read again behind the engine, which waits
for the adoption, as the old reopen-under-engine did. Regression holds a wake
read across a committed adoption; it fails with the fallback removed. (3)
MINOR: the shared-read test now waits for every poll to reach its wait. The
reviewer found no FairMutex handoff, lock-order or permit/share accounting
defect.

## 2026-10-08 — S1: writing the reserved system principal is refused at `check` (LLP 3000.036 §4 A)

Twelve farm builds (11 GPT) wrote `actor: 'system'` or a job's `viewer` into
a principal column. `check` said ok, and the job parked when a schedule fired,
with `E_INPUT: E_INPUT: activity.actor cannot carry the reserved system
principal` in `doctor`. The binder now refuses `E_SYSTEM_PRINCIPAL_WRITE` at
the field, for a `principal`, `principal ?` or `[principal]` column, when the
written value is the literal `'system'` (in any operation), a job's `viewer`
(alone or as a list item; inside `as` writes are already refused), or when a
job insert omits a column whose default is `viewer` or `'system'`:

```
schema.q:23:23 — E_SYSTEM_PRINCIPAL_WRITE: activity.actor cannot store the reserved system principal, and this writes `viewer`, which in a job (outside `as`) is the system: the write can never succeed and would park the job at runtime
  rewrite: make the column optional and write null for system events (`actor: principal ?`, then `actor: null`), or name a service principal (`actor: 'service:reminders'`)
  guide: jobs
```

This is the one item that narrows what `check` accepts: a never-invoked job
holding such a write now fails `check`. It preserves every runtime outcome,
since the write could never succeed. Values that reach the column through a
local or an argument stay a runtime refusal (the engine check is unchanged and
remains the backstop). The code is in `guide::CODES` and `guide jobs`.
Ticket `…-reserved-system-principal-compiles-then-parks` is closed. The doubled
`E_INPUT: E_INPUT:` prefix in the stored run error is not changed here: it
would change the wire `message` of every E_INPUT refusal.

Review (lane S1, all four commits): one blind GPT-6 Astra review at xhigh,
three rounds. Round 1, NOT READY, six findings, all folded:
- An upsert's insert arm runs only when the row is absent, so the
  default-viewer refusal now applies to plain inserts only.
- The principal check skips writes with a spread (a later spread replaces the
  field), immutable columns on update and upsert (dropped against a hidden
  row), and if-absent inserts into a sequence table (a no-op at a full
  sequence).
- `N_WRITE_DENIED` treats immutable fields beside `written by` fields as
  droppable.
- `update <- false` gets the note.
- A recorded non-rule cause (an authorization allowance) keeps its name.
- A forwarded `run` no longer matches the dev record by time.

Round 2, NOT READY, three findings in the trace printer, folded:
- A forwarded `run` picks a record only when every response sequence after its
  pre-send baseline is present and exactly one matches, so a delayed, dropped
  or evicted record prints nothing.
- Only a local `run` quotes source, from the exact captured files it compiled.
  A forwarded `run` prints the recorded cause, site and generation, and the
  dev record now carries `siteKind` so an omitted rule is named without
  source.
- Comment stripping is quote-aware.

Round 3: READY.

## 2026-10-08 — A predicted insert over an unheld supplied id is documented, not prevented

The device oracle's two `write-predicted-refused` cases (slice C) are a plain
`insert` whose caller-supplied id names another owner's row on a `sync to
.owner` table. The device predicts it, the server refuses `E_RULE`, and
settlement withdraws the row. A first lane made the device prove such an id
absent before predicting (WIP `628596dec9`, not landed). That broke 67 device
tests and paved guide forms, because every literal or argument id on a
private, membership or horizon table lost its prediction; a chat client that
mints its own row ids would stop seeing its sends.

Charlie ruled for the other option: keep the prediction and say what can
happen. The `prediction` card's Refusals section and `contract.ts`'s `Write`
comment now state that a plain insert with a supplied id predicts without
proving it absent, that a row the device cannot read with that id makes the
server refuse `E_RULE` and settlement withdraw the pending row, and that ids
minted for the call never collide this way. The card holds its 368-line
budget by dropping two doubled blank lines.

The harness gains a third kind of verdict, `Named`, for a documented outcome
recognised by an exact condition. `predicted-then-refused-unheld-id` requires
an insert, a prediction of `items/<key>`, an `E_RULE` refusal, a server row
with that id that neither the viewer's server read nor the device's
pre-admission read shows, and passing convergence. It is never a pass. A
hidden collision on a secondary unique key under a fresh id is still a
disagreement. The two retained cases replay as the name. Seeds 0–19,999:
433 compared writes per store, 422 passed, 11 named, 1,950 not compared
(1,821 unsynced table, 129 declined), zero write disagreements.

## 2026-10-08 — The Lean oracle: emitter, runner and `run-lean` (LLP 3000.035 §5.2)

Lane LO built the comparison of the engine with the Lean model.

- **Emitter.** `snapback4_lang::emit::lean` translates a checked program's
  *surface* tree to the model's case JSON (`lean/README.md`). It never reads
  the binder's IR, so the binder stays under test. The few types it needs
  come from the declarations the checker accepted: a text literal beside an
  id is an id, and positional keys choose the unique key whose types accept
  them. Anything else is a named reason, never a partial translation.
  `snapback4 check --emit-lean <file.q>` prints one file.
- **Runner.** `quarry-oracle` (`lean/Oracle.lean`, I/O in
  `Quarry/CaseJson.lean`): a JSON case per line in, a tagged outcome per line
  out, one process per worker. `lean/check.sh` now also diffs it against a
  fixture.
- **Oracle.** `snapback4-difftest run-lean` compares the following and
  shrinks to `lean--{field}--{engine}~{model}`:
  - kind, refusal code, tagged data, `complete` and `next` presence;
  - each side's own continuation;
  - a mutation's `observe` reread, run on each side's resulting store.

  `lean::generate` adds Lean-only variants to half the seeds, aimed at
  `OPEN.md`: per-effect and named update rules, a hidden probe target,
  nullable and id orders, and residual filters. The generator AST gained
  three serde-defaulted fields, so older artifacts still load.
- **Nightly.** `difftest-scheduled.py` builds the oracle with `lake` before
  any campaign, and fails the run when Lean is missing. It adds calibration
  and campaign steps for `run-lean`. One-time host setup (elan, no sudo) is
  in AGENTS.md. Nothing was changed on expo-build-450a.

**Run.** 60,000 cases, 8 workers, release, 62 s:

- 91.0% supported; the unsupported 9.0% are `sum`, `min` and `max`;
- 53,277 agree and 1,321 disagree, under four signatures.

**Negative controls.** Two planted faults were each caught, then reverted:

- `or` evaluating its right side: 241 in 2,000 cases. It had to be planted
  in the binder's `or` lowering; the interpreter's short-circuit is never
  reached.
- `items`' read rule skipped in `check_rule`: 79 cases under five new
  signatures in 2,000 (leaked point reads, hidden rows on non-uniform scans,
  changed write refusals).

**What it found:**

- **R2, open and security-relevant.** The engine judges an unnamed
  `update <- R` on the next image only. `update <- .owner = viewer` therefore
  lets a viewer take over another principal's row with a blind
  `upsert`/`update` that sets `owner: viewer`. The model refuses. Named rules
  agree.
- **C2, open.** Non-uniform and residual-filter pages that fill carry `next`
  with nothing after it.
- **A model defect, fixed by LLP 3000.027 §1.** A cursorless top-N page has
  no `next`. This is now OPEN C9, confirmed.

The engine agreed with the model's choices on R1, V2, V3, V5, C1, C8, W1, W3
and W7. Tickets for the four open signatures are in `issues/`.

- **What felt good:** the model's executable semantics made each
  disagreement a one-line diagnosis. Tagged values caught nothing new here,
  but would catch any id/text confusion.
- **What was surprising:** both planted faults had to move. The interpreter
  paths I would have guessed (`Binary` short-circuit,
  `read_authority_inner`) are not where server reads decide. A negative
  control is only meaningful once the planted line is shown to be on the
  path.

## 2026-10-08 — An unnamed update rule judges old and next (security fix; Lean OPEN R2)

The Lean oracle's R2 disagreement was an engine defect, not an open question.
The rules card and `why NOT_FOUND` say "the update rule judges old and next",
but the engine judged an unnamed `update <- R` against the next image only.
`update <- .owner = viewer` without `immutable owner` therefore let any caller
`update` or `upsert` another principal's row with `owner: viewer` and take
it, even a row it could not read. **This is a security fix and must be
published.**

- **Root cause.** The binder binds `.col` in an unnamed rule to
  `RuleTerm::Field`, which the evaluator reads from the next image, and
  `Runner::check_rule` evaluated the update rule as bound. Named
  `update (old, next)` rules were right all along (374 of 374 agreed).
- **Fix.** `schema/update_images.rs` gives `RuleExpr::old_and_next` (the
  rule over the old image, then over the next) and `Table::judges_old_image`.
  `check_rule` applies it to every update and upsert-patch arm, so the
  server's SQLite and Postgres stores and the device's prediction (one
  evaluator) all judge both images. Target resolution prepays both images'
  probes. A rule reading only `id` and immutable columns is still judged
  once: both images agree there, and the decision is static, so the meter
  never depends on the row. Refusals follow the table: `E_RULE` on a
  readable target, `NOT_FOUND` with no detail on an unreadable one.
- **Analyses kept consistent.** `N_MAINTAIN_DELTA`'s "old-image guard
  entails the read rule" proof now sees the unnamed rule's old image;
  `check --cost` and the scale report list the probes the engine prepays.
  Residency sites, `N_WRITE_DENIED`, field authority and own-key proofs read
  the same columns and stay sound (both images is strictly narrower).
- **Tests.** `snapback4-core/tests/update_rule_images.rs` (the four probe
  variants refuse and leave bob's row unchanged; the owner still writes; a
  named next-only rule behaves as written; a probe rule judges the old group;
  a device does not predict the takeover) and the Postgres test
  `engine::postgres::tests::update_images`. Both fail on the old engine.
- **Harness.** Both shrunk cases replay as agreeing and are kept as resolved
  regressions. `run-lean --seed 0 --cases 20,000`: 394 disagreements, all C2
  (`next--next~no-next` 250, `continuation-next--next~no-next` 144); main
  had 421, including `committed~NOT_FOUND` 24 and `committed~E_RULE` 3.
  `run-devices` (5,000) is identical to main (only the known heap-bytes cut
  signatures); the default `run` (5,000) has no disagreement.
- **wasm.** 645,374 → 645,929 B gzip (+555; budget 646,180 unchanged). A
  first spelling with `Cow` and `BTreeSet`s cost +2,747 and went over;
  folding images in place behind one `dyn FnMut` and scanning constraints
  directly brought it under.
- **What was surprising:** the paved form pairs `update <- .authorId =
  viewer` with `immutable authorId`, where the two readings coincide, so the
  card examples never showed the gap. A scan found the unpaired owner form in
  dozens of fixtures, starters, guide cards and reports; no app, starter or
  card relied on judging the next image only. One test did: the security
  review's `hidden_put_uses_update_authority_and_old_owner_can_deny_it`
  (`snapback4-sim/tests/security.rs`) expected bob's blind `upsert` under
  the unnamed `update <- .owner = viewer` to take alice's hidden account. It
  now spells that grant as `update (old, next) <- next.owner = viewer`, and
  the unnamed rule refuses `NOT_FOUND`. `page_admission`'s update variant now
  prepays two rule probes, one per image, because its `group` is mutable.

Landing note: the wasm budget rises from 646,180 to 646,816 B gzip. Rebased
on the heap-uniform landing `9d5e158aa1`, the combined device measures
646,316 B on macOS, 136 B over. The fix's own cost was already cut from
+2,747 to +555 B. Per the ratchet rule, the budget is raised in the same
commit with the reason in `metrics/wasm-budget.json`: this macOS measurement
plus 500 B. macOS measures at or above Linux. This fix must be published.

## 2026-10-08 — The difftest generator is widened (LLP 3000.035 §5.1, lane GW)

Branch `sb4/difftest-widen`. `snapback4-difftest/src/widen.rs` adds what
slice A left out. It draws from a stream independent of the base generator
(`generate::base`), so an unwidened seed is the base case byte for byte.

**What it adds** (frequencies over seeds 0–19,999):

- prefetch-reachable reads, 21.8%: pages projecting `tags[.tag]` and
  `tags[name = .label]`, and a loop reading `tags[row.tag]`;
- mutation blocks, 12.3%: lets, `require`, `if`/`else`, several writes to
  `key` and `k2`, and reads after writes;
- a prelude of mutations on the same store, 17.1%: compared on every oracle,
  sometimes as the other viewer; a device catches up by one sync round;
- expiry, 16.8%: a clock advancing between operations, sweeps and
  `until: now + ttl`;
- upsert insert-arm clashes on a seeded `tag` (OPEN W4).

The other changes:

- the shrinker reduces each new shape, and now skips reductions that change
  nothing (they looped forever);
- `lean::generate` narrows half the out-of-fragment cases back in;
- `snapback4-difftest compile <file.q>` prints binder diagnostics.

**Prefetch.** The ticket's planted fault (first consumed hit becomes a miss)
was caught by the random corpus: 1,523 prefetch-on disagreements in 2,000
seeds, none prefetch-off. After the revert there were 0, and
`git diff --quiet` was clean on core, device and bind. Over 20,000 seeds:

- 1,957 cases transferred rows;
- 619,942 rows were transferred;
- 49,523 probes consumed cached answers (fewer database calls with prefetch
  on).

The coverage ticket is closed.

**20,000-case runs.** Stores and `run` agree everywhere. Devices: 780
disagreements per store. Lean: 2,552 disagreements. Each new signature is
retained under `cases/found/` with a DIAGNOSIS.md, and grouped into five
tickets:

- unswept expired rows: the server's meter counts them and the device's does
  not;
- a device prediction over a hidden secondary unique clash;
- a device's final refusal after an unproved prediction carries a later
  statement's code;
- the Lean model's field-of-null defect (OPEN E4, 2,221 cases; the fix is
  owed, since this lane was not permitted to change the model);
- R2 and W4 reached under new signatures.

**Harness defects fixed:**

- commute's cost claim did not hold when the right operand hoists a read;
- the prelude's source sites moved under rewrites, so the prelude is now
  emitted first;
- the pending marker was not stripped inside `observe`'s array;
- the unheld-id named outcome did not recognise a one-insert block;
- coverage counted a delete's unused value.

- **What felt good:** the independent stream made the widening safe to land
  without disturbing existing pins. The physical database-call witness gave
  consumption coverage without touching the engine.
- **What was hard:** one model defect (field of null) produced twelve
  signatures by engine class, and one expiry meter difference produced
  fourteen per device store. The signature scheme splits a cause by its
  surface, so a diagnosis has to regroup them.
- **What was surprising:** the binder's left-spill makes `2 + read` cost two
  more steps than `read + 2`. Commute was never cost-free once operands could
  read.

## 2026-10-11 — Workstream B: rule-language friction from the wave 1 app farm (LLP 3000.036 §11)

The 100-lane farm on 0.4.16 (`~/sb4-loop/wave1/analysis/patterns.md`) kept
hitting the same rule-language walls. This entry is workstream B's pass; the
decisions are recorded in LLP 3000.036 §11.

- **Rules say what they evaluate.** `E_QUARRY_RULE_OPERATOR` replaces
  `E_QUARRY_UNKNOWN` ("ordered comparisons belong to update transitions",
  whose rewrite was the chat app's `readUpTo`). It covers `now`, arithmetic,
  helper calls and misplaced ordered comparisons, and its rewrite is the
  author's own comparison as a mutation `require … else INVALID_<FIELD>`.
  Insert rules may now order the row's own required int/time columns
  (`.stars >= 1`), behind the `insert-rule-order` capability. `guide rules`
  opens with a table of rule forms.
- **Messages and reserved words.** `require … else CODE 'message'` and
  `! else CODE 'message'` carry the message on the wire refusal, as `unique`
  does; a table rule's `else CODE` says rules refuse with E_RULE.
  `E_QUARRY_RESERVED` names `read:`, `by:`, `after:` and `update` as a
  parameter at the declaration, and `snapback4 why E_QUARRY_RESERVED` lists the reserved words.
- **Rewrites from the author's line.** Covered:
  - `N_NEVER_COMPLETE` prints the pin as code: the parent read and
    `.board = cardRow.board`, or one query per party for a two-party rule. It
    also says when a staff grant is not used.
  - The constraint form of `E_STRUCTURAL_FANOUT` offers a count view over the
    author's own table.
  - Also: `E_QUARRY_BOUND` on a total, the read-rule hop (table-rule repair
    rather than mutation syntax), the sync window without dots, sum clause
    order, `1w`, `not a = b`, the nested-predicate `.` scope, and the
    `.id = .ref` probe key.
- **Accepted forms.** Now accepted:
  - `t[row]` reads by the row's id.
  - A page inside an object ends at the next `field:`.
  - Named equalities covering two total unique keys choose the first key.
- **Defects.** Lane 081's job sweep no longer reports `$pureCallConstants`,
  and its schedule cascade is hidden. Lane 008's silent 0 from a
  `read <- deny` maintain is now `N_READ_DENIED`.
- **Deferred.** A `require`/grant-proven role as a completeness proof (#28):
  it changes the engine's page verdict, the device and the Lean oracle's
  `complete`. That is the lead session's call. The note and `guide bounds`
  ("Private lists") say what staff get instead.

- **What felt good:** most of the friction was rewrite text, fixable in the
  binder with the source already in hand.
- **What was hard:** existing tests pin some wording on purpose (the
  constraint rewrite must not infer booking intent from column names), so the
  new renderings add to that text rather than replace it.

## 2026-10-12 — UNION revision 6: expiry at the commit boundary

Round 5's GPT review found an existing row that moved to a new recipient
while ending its life could name its id to that recipient, immediately and
again at the sweep. Commit retirement now considers changed synced rows as
well as births; commit-start accounting revokes the previous recipients
without announcing the expired image to a new one. The regression checks
Bob's revocation and Mallory's empty stream at page sizes 1 and 1,000 before
and after a sweep. Snapshot catch-up's R2 reads its private staged server
images; ordinary/deferred stream application first withdraws predictions.
The web build also needed the audience-epoch helper's Table type qualified
outside the SQLite-only import. No wasm behavior changes in that repair.
## 2026-10-12 — A development store reset: `POST /dev/reset` (author-approved)

Test runners can now isolate tests against one running `snapback4 dev`.
`POST /dev/reset` (and `snapback4 reset [--port N] [--seed <fixture dir|rows.json>]
[--clock reset]`) empties the store in one SQLite transaction and can reseed it
with `/seed`'s rows in the same transaction; a refused row resets nothing.
"Fresh" keeps `_meta`, `_catalog` and `_generations` and service seats (the dev
worker's session, `token` seats) and empties every other table it finds, so a
table added later is emptied by default. The store takes a new `store_id`, and
the reset is itself a commit, so the head keeps counting; clients treat it as a
replaced store (local re-acquires, online halts `E_STORE_REPLACED`), and no
client change was needed. The dev clock is kept unless `{"clock":"reset"}`.
`serve` refuses it like `/seed`. A reset with a 20-row reseed takes ~1.4 ms
median over HTTP in the debug build. Design in LLP 3000.007 §20.25; documented
in `guide wire`, `guide testing` (a per-test recipe) and CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS
§5. `Engine::seed_at`'s body moved to `seed_rows` so the reset can run it inside
its own transaction.

- **What felt good:** the client side already handled a replaced store end to
  end; the reset only had to look like one.
- **What was hard:** choosing what survives. Personas need no rows, but the dev
  worker holds a real session; keeping `service:` seats is what lets the worker
  keep running across resets.

## 2026-10-12 — File assets: a third kind beside image and video (LLP 3000.038)

App-farm builders of receipts, contracts, sheet music, data rooms and lab
results needed PDFs and were refused. The author approved a `file` type:
`file <=N` or `file <=N ('application/pdf', ...)`, the image contract (one
home, the home row's read rule, release and sweep), no transcoding. LLP
1006 §13a had the deferred design; this lands it with one change, the
per-column allow-list, checked at placement like the byte bound so the
upload stays column-less.

- **Verification.** Only types Snapback can check against the bytes may be
  listed (PDF, plain/CSV/Markdown text, JSON, PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF, zip and the
  three OOXML types); HTML, SVG, XML and JavaScript are compile errors. The
  upload (`POST /assets?as=file&name=`) declares its type in Content-Type;
  a mismatch with the magic number (or invalid UTF-8/JSON for text) is
  E_ASSET_TYPE. Undeclared binaries are named by their bytes; text never is.
- **Bounds.** A file upload streams at most the schema's largest file bound
  (413 E_ASSET_TOO_LARGE, before reading when Content-Length says so).
- **Delivery.** Always an attachment: Content-Disposition with an ASCII
  fallback and RFC 8187 name, nosniff, `default-src 'none'; sandbox`, text
  as `text/plain; charset=utf-8`. HTML uploaded as text/plain is served as
  text. Ranges work; `once` is refused on file columns.
- **Names.** `_assets` gains `name` (added in place to older stores); the
  filename keeps its last segment, loses control and bidi characters and
  leading dots, at most 255 bytes, `file` when empty.
- **Client.** `upload(bytes, { file: {} })`; `asset(id)` and `useAsset`
  report `name`; `saveAsset` (`snapback4/client`) and `useSaveAsset` save on
  demand. The contract gains an optional `UploadOptions` argument and an
  optional `name` on `Asset`/`AssetRead`: additive, proposed here per the
  one-owner rule; nothing existing changes shape.
- **Device.** Upload receipts predict `file` arguments; a receipt of the
  other kind never predicts (the server refuses the kind). Retained files
  keep their name offline.
- **wasm budget rises 2,116 B.** The same Linux build of 3add6058b7 measures
  2,147,888 B raw / 648,672 B gzip; this tree 2,156,339 B / 650,940 B
  (+2,268 B, 1,616 B over 649,324). The bytes are the device's share: two
  serde struct variants (`ColumnType::File`, `ArgType::File` with the
  allow-list), their display and match arms, and the receipt kind check.
  Budget 651,440 B (measurement + 500 B), reason in `metrics/wasm-budget.json`.
- **Deferred.** A native Expo document picker and "save to Files" helper
  (`upload` and `asset` already work with React Native Blobs); audio types;
  HEIC; previews.

## 2026-10-12 — The Lean model catches up, and a pinned parent probe decides a page

Three engine changes of 2026-10-11 (LLP 3000.036 §12.1 readable grants,
§15.4 where guards, §15.12 search `exists`) had landed without the Lean
model, whose hosts had no `lake`. The model now decides a scan by its pins
or by a page guard evaluated over the caller's view, answers a search
`exists` `true` on a visible match, `false` only when decided and otherwise
unavailable, and the emitter translates grants, emits `exists t[key]` as a
point read and applies the compiler's where-guard lowering. `lean::generate`
draws all three from a third independent stream.

Then the deferred §16.3 change: a read-rule disjunct whose row columns the
scan's prefix pins, and whose probed rows its holders can read, is a page
guard on the server (`rules::page_guard_decision`, evaluated once with the
prefix's values), so the board owner's cards and the leader's roster are
`complete: true`. `check` follows `if`/`require` on the pinned probe, the
copy-the-principal recipe is gone, devices are unchanged (a union rule
cannot sync). The model's C8 gained the same arm with `Rule.eval_pin`,
`granted_readable` and `decided_store`; `./check.sh` audits 46 theorems and
runs 42 examples, and `run-lean` over 100,000 cases shows only the
classified C2/W4 signatures. The web device grows 578 B gzip (649,250 B,
inside the 649,324 B budget) after sharing the grant and prefix-row code.
The ticket is closed.

## 2026-10-12 — UNION revision 7: epoch transitions compose with acquisition

GPT's sixth blind review found obsolete-scope filtering could invalidate
window marker positions, and a first post-epoch continuous renewal could
miss a deletion beside it. Filtering now precedes expansion, while the raw
watermark passes removed scopes. Internal joins record a pre-commit
renewal's previous deadline; same-commit births carry no predecessor.
A currently live acquisition replaces its until-revoked group before
putting current rows, so an expired replacement or an older join lacking
metadata cannot preserve stale snapshot rows. Continuous renewals keep
their existing rows and boundaries; a scope names only the acquired group,
never an id deleted in the acquiring commit. R2 keeps column-arm rows.
The new traces run both real stores at page sizes 1 and 1,000, covering
markers, live renewal, expired replacement and genuine acquisition.

## 2026-10-12 — Referential actions: a reference declares what deleting its row does (LLP 3000.039)

The author asked for the end-game answer to LLP 3000.036 §15.8. A reference
column now says `on delete restrict | cascade | set null | keep`; an
undeclared one is `restrict`, so deleting a row a live row still references
refuses `E_REFERENCED` naming the referencing column. This is a deliberate
behavior change (no users depend on stability): `check` names every delete
it changes (`N_DELETE_RESTRICTED`, replacing `N_DELETE_ORPHANS`), `on delete
keep` restores the old meaning, and `keep` is spelled by absence in the
schema, so all-keep schemas stay byte-identical and capability-free.

- **Design**, reviewed blind three rounds (GPT gpt-6.1-sol and Muse
  muse-spark-1.3-contributor; records under `llp/reviews/3000.039-*`): the
  parent's delete authorizes a declared cascade or set null; a delete closes
  over cascades, probes restrict references outside the closure (reporting
  the first occupied one in schema order), clears set-null references
  outside it and removes children first, each from its current image; set
  null only on optional references no rule of any table reads; cascade and
  set null need `cap N by <reference>` and a schema-fixed reservation that
  `check` proves fits (`E_CASCADE_BOUND`); every published trace (meter,
  touched tables, change footprint, event count, physical allowance) is
  schema-fixed; a device predicts only over referencing groups it holds
  current and whole, else queues. No background sweep: the recipes (lower
  the cap, a job, mark and sweep) cover unbounded relations.
- **Behavior changes to know**: a table that restrict/cascade/set-null
  references name needs its deleter to read the row (`N_DELETE_NEEDS_READ`
  where the rules' shapes cannot show it); every such reference gets an
  index (`$reference:<column>`), so writes to it maintain one more index —
  the RP calibration's `index_entries` ceilings rose by exactly 2 (README
  amendment). Expiry fires no action.
- **Fixtures that pin legacy bytes** (capability-free control, RX legacy
  identity, recorded attribution, following view, timeline capability,
  maintained columns, derived clique, adoption) spell their references
  `on delete keep`: their frozen meaning. The JS capability fence keeps a
  `legacyOrdinary` source for the published 0.2.33 binary.
- **Verification**: compiler, engine and device unit tests; device scenarios
  on both stores; an exhaustive simulator check of cascades, restrict and
  disclosure over every two-operation sequence (three opt-in); the Lean
  model gains references, `refDelete` and `refDelete_without_actions`
  (35/35 examples); `run-lean` over 100,000 seeds with a `kids` reference
  family (all actions, ~3,800 delete cases compared) finds only the four
  classified open signatures; `run-devices` seeds 0–2999 finds no new
  signature.
- **Wasm budget**: 648,672 → 661,877 B gzip on Linux (+13,205 B); budget
  662,377 B with the reason in `metrics/wasm-budget.json`. About 11 KB is the
  web device predicting the cascade; queueing such deletes on the web only is
  the lever if the diet needs it.

- **What felt good:** the existing held-group proof, reservation plans and
  change-evidence widening gave every soundness requirement a place to live.
- **What was hard:** disclosure is everywhere a delete is observable — the
  meter, the touched tables, footprints, event counts, the physical
  allowance, refusal order — and each review round found another channel.
- **Fourth round** (revision 3 with its code; GPT NOT READY, Muse READY WITH
  CHANGES): the code fell short of its own reservation and two interactions
  leaked or corrupted. Fixed: walks stream four-row pages and keep identities
  only (a restrict probe streams a row per seek past the closure, the root
  included — a self-referencing root had hidden an outside holder); set null
  rereads each row before clearing it (a buffered image overwrote another
  clear's maintained count); the reply's event count is decided by the
  static action envelope, not by which rows actions reached; the reservation
  prices the pages and charges output. The shipped Following recipe's
  `feed.eventId` now says `on delete keep` (its inbox purges lazily behind
  tombstones; the new restrict default refused `deletePost`). run-lean 100k
  and run-devices 0–2999 match the earlier runs signature for signature;
  wasm 662,137 B gzip, within the raised budget.

## 2026-10-12 — ROLL: retaining rollback and hot release activation

Release adoption now separates active shapes from dormant tables/cells/index definitions. Older writes preserve retained cells; new rows get candidate literal defaults/nulls on restoration, while enum, required-value, ownership and lifetime conflicts name affected rows and refuse atomically. Removal requires explicit `prune --allow-destructive`, with durable audit/history. `rollback --to N` deliberately restores immutable source. Release stores get a format fence; device/development stores retain their existing format.

Native wasm content changes advance semantic generation even when declarations are unchanged. Worker preparation is revision-bound, including named additions/removals. ## 2026-10-12 — Lane EX: the meter charges only live rows; a refusal after an unproved insert defers to the server

Two findings of the widened generator (LLP 3000.035 §5.1), branch
`sb4/device-meter-expiry`.

- **Ruling A (Charlie, 2026-10-08), LLP 3000.007 §20.24.6.** The public meter
  charges only rows live at the read's clock. The server's scans charged an
  expired row the sweep had not removed (examined, then steps and heap), which
  the device never received, so meters diverged and low ceilings cut on the
  server where the device completed. Now `scan_authorized` (both paths, a
  system read through a new `live_store_scan`), the private authorization walk,
  the device's live recount and the server's maintained backlog read step over
  expired rows before any public charge. `Runner::step_expired` prices them on
  their own guard (256 B plus key per row, `E_STORE_MEMORY` past 256 MiB per
  execution) and returns their unit of the 8,192-row walk. One engine change
  covers SQLite, PostgreSQL, `MemoryRows` and both device stores.
- **Defect B, LLP 3000.007 §20.5.** A device predicted an insert over a hidden
  id or unique value, carried on, and refused locally later in the block
  (`E_CONSTRAINT`, `NOT_FOUND`, `E_OVERFLOW`), a final code the server never
  reports (it refuses `E_RULE` at the insert). Each authored plain device insert
  now runs the upsert insert-arm proof on the device allowance; after an
  unproved one, `predict` turns a later refusal into `E_PREDICT`, so the write
  queues and the server's refusal is reported. Provable refusals stay final.
- **Tests.** Four focused tests in `snapback4-difftest/tests/devices.rs` (server
  against both device stores at every boundary of every dimension; a cut before
  and after the sweep; the three refusal shapes queue; provable refusals stay
  local); all fail on the old engine. About thirty tests pinned the old model
  (expired rows charged, backlogs cutting reads or refusing `E_BOUND`, literal-id
  inserts refusing locally) and now state the new contract; where a backlog was
  only a device to force a cut, a rejected live row or a lower ceiling does it.
- **Harness (main's widened generator).** `run-devices --seed 0 --cases 20000`:
  0 read and 0 cut disagreements in 152,256 positions per store (the 14 expired-meter
  signatures per store are gone); writes: 11 named unique-key outcomes per store
  and 1 disagreement per store, the known insert beside an `upsert` branch
  (outside the named condition, recorded in the GW follow-up); the three
  `write-refused` signatures are gone. `run-stores --seed 0 --cases 5000` with a
  private PostgreSQL 17 cluster: 0 disagreements (128,202 positions per prefetch
  mode, 1,124 prelude, 3,964,936 SQLite repeats). The 30 retained device cases
  replay as resolved regressions (`pass`, or `prediction-declined` for the
  refusals).
- **wasm.** 646,316 → 646,816 B gzip (+500; budget 646,816 unchanged, zero
  headroom). The first spelling cost +2,363; compaction: a web device never reads
  as the system, so `live_store_scan` is SQLite-only; the step price is a fixed
  reservation, not a serialized row size; `device_work` split into non-generic
  enter/leave halves (−157 across its instantiations); B reuses
  `prove_upsert_insert` instead of a refactored proof; short messages.
- **What was surprising:** the meter used to carry a time-hidden existence bit
  (a word held only by an expired row cost a seek; a maintained backlog cost
  observable examined work). The ruling closes it; the attack witness in
  `expiring_mutations.rs` now shows the worlds agree even without the admission
  guard.
- **What was hard:** the collateral. Literal-id inserts into partitioned tables
  are common in tests, so B changed the expected outcome of every such test
  whose program refuses after the insert. The wasm budget had 500 B of room.
